title: Ourang Medan: The Ghost Ship That Whispered 'I Die'
description:
A ship sends a desperate SOS that ends with the words I die. When rescuers board, the whole crew is said to be dead, their eyes open and faces frozen in shock.

This case file follows the legend of the Ourang Medan from its first appearance in an Italian newspaper in 1940 to the later versions, and weighs the theories of poison gas and carbon monoxide against the fact that no record of the ship has ever been found.

Do you think the Ourang Medan was real, or a story told too well? Tell us in the comments.

shots.text: A radio operator taps out a message in Morse code, and the last words he sends are, I die.
Then the signal goes silent, and the ship drifts on alone.
When help finally arrives, every person aboard is dead, and nobody can say what killed them.
This is case file number 3.

shots.text: The story begins in the Pacific, in the autumn of 1940, with a newspaper in the Italian city of Trieste.
A series of articles called the dramas of the sea told of a steamship named Ourang Medan.
The name is Malay, and it roughly means man of Medan, after the large city on Sumatra.
According to that first version, a distress signal went out from waters south of the Solomon Islands.
The first message read, S.O.S. from the steamship Ourang Medan, and begged for a doctor.
A second message followed, saying the second officer was probably dead, and that other crew members were also killed.
It ended with a plea for a warship, and then a final, unfinished phrase.
The words were, crew has, and then nothing more.
Ships that answered the call received no reply at all.
Imagine the radio room of a nearby ship, where an operator listens through the static, hoping he has misheard.
The words were clear enough, and every minute that passed made the silence feel heavier.
Hold on to that detail, because the story would not stay the same for long.

shots.text: In the version told in 1948, the setting moves to the Straits of Malacca.
Two American vessels, the Silver Star and the City of Baltimore, are said to have heard the call.
In this telling, the message was longer and far more desperate.
It said that all the officers, including the captain, lay dead in the chartroom and on the bridge.
It said that probably the whole crew was dead.
Then came a few broken dots and dashes, and the words, I die.
The crew of the Silver Star found the ship, and boarded her.
She looked undamaged, floating calmly under a bright sun.
But the decks were littered with the dead, even the ship's dog.
Their faces were turned up toward the sky, mouths open, eyes staring straight ahead.
Those who found them said the crew looked frightened, as if they had seen something terrible.
There were no wounds, and no visible sign of what had happened.
Nothing in the account says anyone searched for a cause before the danger came.
There were no survivors to ask.

shots.text: The rescuers decided to tow the silent ship to the nearest port.
They began to prepare the lines, and the crew of the Silver Star worked quickly.
Then, suddenly, a fire broke out in the number four cargo hold.
Smoke rose from below, and the boarding party hurried back to their own vessel.
The captain of the rescue ship had no choice but to call everyone back.
Any further search of the Ourang Medan was now impossible.
Some versions say the ship exploded.
Soon afterward, she slipped beneath the waves.
And with her went the only chance of finding out what had happened.
The 1940 version tells it differently, with explosions heard as rescuers explored the ship, and a blaze that sank her in the Pacific.

shots.text: Some tellings add one more figure, an unnamed German sailor from the crew.
He is said to have swum to safety, and to have been found on Taongi Atoll in the Marshall Islands.
An Italian missionary and local people are said to have found him.
Before he died, the man supposedly told the missionary what the ship had been carrying.
He spoke of a badly stowed cargo of oil of vitriol, with poisonous fumes escaping from broken containers.
The ship, he said, was sailing from a small Chinese port toward Costa Rica, and had deliberately avoided the authorities.
It is a vivid detail, yet it appears only in later versions of the tale.

shots.text: Over the years, people have offered theories to explain the deaths.
One theory, put forward by Roy Bainton and others, is that the ship carried smuggled chemicals.
They suggest a mix such as potassium cyanide and nitroglycerin, or even leftover wartime nerve agents.
In this theory, sea water entered the hold and reacted with the cargo, releasing toxic gas.
The crew would have been overcome, and the same water might later have caused the fire and the explosion.
A related idea claims the cargo was tabun, a nerve gas stored by Japan in China during the war.
It says the gas had been handed to the American military, and was moved on an unregistered ship to leave no paper trail.
Another theory, from the writer Vincent Gaddis, is far simpler.
He suggests an undetected fire or a fault in the boiler system, releasing carbon monoxide.
The gas would have killed everyone aboard, while the fire slowly spread until it destroyed the ship.
These are only theories, and none of them has ever been proven.

shots.text: And here the story begins to come apart.
Researchers have searched Lloyd's Register, the great record of the world's ships, and found no mention of the Ourang Medan.
No registration for a ship of that name has been found, in the Netherlands or in any other country searched.
The logs of the Silver Star show no record of any rescue attempt.
Even the date and place keep moving, from 1940 to 1947 to 1948, and from the Solomon Islands to the Straits of Malacca.
When a Dutch newspaper printed the story in 1948, it added a warning.
The editors wrote that it may seem obvious the whole thing is fantasy, a thrilling romance of the sea.
Yet the author, Silvio Scherli, a radio operator and journalist, assured them it was true.
So perhaps there was a ship, and a terrible night, and a message that ended with two words.
Or perhaps it was a tale told so well that it sailed around the world.
The sea keeps its secrets, and this one may never be settled.
If a crew could vanish without a record, how many other stories are we missing? Tell us what you think in the comments.

shots.text: An SOS crackles over the radio, and it ends with two words: I die.
Ships race to answer, but the Ourang Medan does not reply.
When sailors board her, the whole crew is dead.
Their eyes are open, and their faces look frozen in shock.
There are no wounds, and no visible sign of what could have happened aboard.
Then a fire breaks out in the hold, and the boarders flee.
The ship sinks, taking her secrets with her.
But no record of the ship has ever been found.
Some say poison gas leaked from a smuggled cargo, others say a hidden fire released carbon monoxide.
Or was it only a story, told so well that it sailed around the world?

The Ourang Medan may never have existed, yet the story refuses to sink.
